title: GPX Route Stats: Distance and Summary
description: Summarise a GPX file's route geometry with GPX Route Stats — path length and the headline numbers for training logs. Free, in your browser.
summary_sentence: For example, a four-point park loop whose segments run 0.656, 0.749 and 0.656 kilometres reports a path length of 2.06 kilometres — every stats page on Earth is this addition, scaled up.
quick_answer: GPX Route Stats loads a GPX file and summarises its route geometry — path length first among the headline numbers — for training logs and quick briefings. Drop the file locally and read the summary — what the recording covers, without a full GIS or training platform.
steps_intro: The file's headline numbers, honestly labelled:

body.t: The distance line of a log entry, from the file itself — then depth from the specialists:
Two candidate loops, one summary each: lengths side by side settle the 'which is longer?' question before legs vote.
Your platform's distance and your file's geometry occasionally disagree (smoothing, gap handling). The file's own sum is the reference both should answer to.
“Saturday's route: this long, this shape” — a stats summary is the sentence a ride leader needs, extracted in seconds.

Length is the sum of great-circle hops between consecutive points: 0.656 + 0.749 + 0.656 = 2.06 km for the worked loop. Dense recordings trace curves faithfully; sparse ones cut corners — literally — and under-measure winding paths.

A switchbacking trail recorded every 30 seconds reads shorter than the same trail at 1-second density: straight hops chord across the bends. Length is a function of sampling, a truth every stats page inherits.

popular_table.note: Stats are computed from the file as recorded — no smoothing, no gap-filling, no platform seasoning. That rawness is the point: every other number can be audited back to this one.

faq: Both geometries carry length; the summary treats the file's path elements as the route it holds. Recordings and plans read by the same geometry — their authority differs, their arithmetic does not.
Why is the distance shorter than the signposted trail?
Corner-cutting from sparse sampling, GPS shortcuts across switchbacks, or a trail whose sign counts a spur you skipped. The file measures where the device went, at the density it sampled.
Kilometres and miles both, per this site's convention. The underlying sum is metric; the display serves both audiences.
Does it count stopped time or pauses?
Length does not care about time at all — a paused hour adds zero metres. Time statistics live in the duration and speed tools.
The summary covers the file's geometry as a whole; per-track breakdowns follow from splitting or merging deliberately with the family's tools.
Length is horizontal (map) distance, the universal convention — slope distance overstates travel and nobody's odometer uses it. Vertical totals live in the elevation tools.
Consumer recordings typically land within a percent or two of truth on open ground; urban canyons and forests worsen it, and sampling density bends winding routes downward.
